title: Factor-two subtour-LP gap for asymmetric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\le2\,\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) for every integer \(n\ge2\) and every nonnegative directed metric \(c\) on \(n\) vertices with \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)>0\), using the Hamiltonian-tour objective and degree-constrained subtour linear program below? Equivalently, is the universal integrality gap \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=2\), since the matching lower bound is known? This is an existence inequality; no efficient rounding algorithm is required.
why: Would identify the fundamental relaxation gap for asymmetric travelling salesman.
status_note: The checked 2024 book explicitly poses the factor-2 question. The June 2026 primary revision reports finite half-integral computations and the general lower/upper gap, not a resolution. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established factor-2 proof or counterexample. The 6 November 2026 formulation restores the factor-two conjecture. The recorded status checks retain their original dates and scope.
review_note: Defined the complete directed metric, Hamiltonian tour and all constraints of the subtour LP, including zero-cost conventions. Corrected the source context to include the later 17 bound and checked its LP-model equivalence. Distinguished a universal integrality theorem from an efficient approximation algorithm and from restricted enumeration.

sentences: An asymmetric traveling-salesman tour visits every city once, and travel costs may depend on direction.
The subtour linear program permits fractional arcs while enforcing degree and cut constraints.
The card asks whether an optimal tour always costs at most twice this fractional optimum.
The factor concerns the strength of this specific relaxation and does not require an efficient construction.
The directed-metric model is distinct from the symmetric traveling-salesman conjecture.

upgraded_from.title: The factor-2 integrality-gap conjecture for the ATSP subtour LP

definitions:
A directed metric is a function \(c:V	imes V	o\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(c(i,i)=0\) and \(c(i,k)\le c(i,j)+c(j,k)\) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc \((i,j)\) for each \(i
e j\) and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) is the minimum over all such cycles. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta ^{+}(S)=\{(i,j):i\in S,j
otin S\}\) and \(\delta ^{-}(S)=\{(i,j):i
otin S,j\in S\}\); for a set of arcs F write \(x(F)=\sum_{(i,j)\in F} x_{ij}\). \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) minimizes \(\sum_{i
e j} c(i,j)x_{ij}\) over real variables \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) subject to \(x(\delta ^{+}(\{v\}))=x(\delta ^{-}(\{v\}))=1\) for every v, and \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))\ge 1\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\). The degree equalities imply \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))=x(\delta ^{-}(S))\), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. Zero-LP instances are excluded from the ratio; they also have zero tour optimum. Indeed, the positive support of a zero-cost feasible solution is strongly connected by the cut constraints, and directed triangle inequalities then give zero distance between every ordered pair. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)/\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path. The supremum is over every finite size and is not required to be attained. The usual factor-two conjecture asserts \(\Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}=2\), taking account of known approaching lower-bound families.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.

context_blocks.text: The selected binary question is the factor-two subtour-LP integrality-gap conjecture. A proof of the universal inequality or one instance with a strictly larger ratio answers it; a complete determination of any alternative gap is not required.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in \(\{0,1/2,1\}\). An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical \(4/3\) conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.
